en: The Sūtra on the Discernment of the Retribution of Good and Evil, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mingjiao, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Tianxi, at the Mi-lin Monastery in the Kingdom of Jālandhara, Central India.
Translated by Zai Feng. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then, at the time for eating, the Blessed One put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in sequence. He arrived at the house of the householder Śuka, son of Dhanika, and stood outside the gate.
At that time, the householder Śuka had a dog named Śaṅkha who was always at the entrance of his gate.
Thereupon, the householder would regularly place fine rice in a copper vessel and give it to Śaṅkha to eat.
Seeing the World-Honored One, the dog barked out of anger.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Śaṅkha,
"Because you have not yet attained realization, you bark at me."
When these words were spoken, Śaṅkha’s evil mind turned toward malice and resentment; he immediately left his original place and went beneath the sandalwood throne.
At that time, the elder Śuka came out from the door of his house and saw the dog beneath the sandalwood throne.
The elder asked, "Who has provoked your anger?"
Śaṅkha remained silent.
Then the elder Śuka asked again: "Worthy son!
"Who was it that provoked your anger, Śaṅkha?
He replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama came here and stood at the gate; seeing him, I barked."
"That śramaṇa Gautama spoke these words:
'Because you have not yet awakened, you now bark once more.
Upon hearing these words, anger arose in my heart; I rose from my original place and came beneath this sandalwood throne."
At that time, having heard these words, Śuka became greatly incensed and departed from the city of Śrāvastī, proceeding to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that moment, the World-Honored One was seated, surrounded before and behind by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One saw from afar that the householder Śuka was approaching along the road, and he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this householder Śuka coming from afar?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed, we have seen it.
The World-Honored One said:
"This son of a householder directed a mind of anger toward the Buddha; at the end of his life, in a moment as swift as a flying arrow, he fell into the great hell. Why is this?"

Through false and deluded conceptualization, they discriminate between self and other; giving rise to the affliction of anger, they slander the Buddha and fall into the various evil realms to undergo immeasurable suffering.
Furthermore, they give rise to contempt and slander toward me, and all sentient beings do likewise.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus and spoke in verse:
"Those who harbor ill will toward the Buddha, Who slander him and treat him with contempt,
Shall enter the great hells, Where they suffer without end."
There are certain individuals who, having conceived an evil thought for even a moment toward their teacher or a bhikṣu, fall into hell at the end of their lives.
If one gives rise to a heart of great malice and resentment toward the Tathāgata, [the retribution is even more severe].
"All shall fall into the evil realms, Cycling through saṃsāra and constantly suffering.

At that time, the son of Dhanika came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and before the World-Honored One, he praised the Tathāgata with various words that were gentle, kind, and compliant.
Having spoken these words, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions have you come to my house?"
The Buddha told the householder Sūka:

"The time for the meal has arrived; I have put on my robes, taken my bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in sequence, eventually arriving at your residence and standing at your gate."
At that time, Śaṅkha was at the entrance, in the midst of eating and drinking from a bronze vessel; seeing me standing at the door, he barked as soon as he saw me.
I said: "Śaṅkha! Since you have not yet awakened, why do you see a dog?"
Upon hearing these words, the dog became enraged and went to another place.
At that time, the householder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I do not know what the past karmic causes of this dog, Śaṅkha, may have been."
"I pray that the Buddha will expound this. The Buddha said,
"Cease for now!"
"Do not ask about this matter!
If you were to hear it, your distress would redouble until it becomes unbearable.
Thus the householder Śuka made his request three times, saying to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound this matter for us; we long to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder, saying:
"Listen now attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall now analyze and explain it for you. This dog was the body of your father, Dhanika.

In a past life, he falsely conceived of this body as having no self yet reckoned it as a self; he was stingy, greedy, and envious, failing to practice generosity; he covetously clung to wealth and did not believe in the Triple Gem. Consequently, he fell among the animals, and this dog Śaṅkha is that former householder’s father."
The householder Śuka again addressed the World-Honored One:

"My father, Dhanika, during his lifetime constantly practiced giving, making offerings to the fire-god Agni and to various spirits and deities. His body must have certainly attained rebirth in the Brahma Heaven to enjoy great wealth and happiness; for what reason, then, has he fallen among the animal realm?"
"This matter is difficult to believe.
The Buddha said to the elder:

"Your father, Dhanika, due to such discriminatory thoughts and the arising of false attachments, failed to practice generosity and did not have faith in the Triple Gem; by these causes and conditions, he fell into this state of existence."
He further addressed the householder:
"What I have now spoken may be difficult for you to believe; you should return home and inquire with Śaṅkha.
At that time, the householder took his leave of the Buddha and returned home, whereupon he said upon arrival:
"Śaṅkha! It is true that you are my father, Dhanin!
At this, the dog sat down upon the sandalwood throne.
The elder spoke again:
"Śaṅkha! Is it truly my father, Dhanika?"
"You may eat this meat and rice from the copper platter. Śaṅkha then ate it.
Having finished eating, [the deity] spoke again:
"If my father were truly Dhanika, what sign would manifest to demonstrate this wonder?

When Śaṅkha heard these words, he rose from his seat and went to his own dwelling. There, beneath a sandalwood throne, he sniffed the ground with his trunk and dug it up with his feet, revealing four great iron jars filled with gold vessels, platters, and various utensils.
At that time, the elder Śuka, beholding these rare and marvelous treasures of gold, silver, and precious gems, was filled with leaping joy and affectionately protected and concealed them.
Thereupon, the elder departed from the city of Śrāvastī and went to the place where the Buddha was, taking refuge in him with a single-minded devotion.
At that time, the World-Honored One was seated with an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see Śuka, the son of the householder Dhanika, coming from afar?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed, we have seen it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Now that this elder has passed away and his life has ended, he is like one who has cast off a heavy burden and been reborn in the heavens; because he felt such joy and exultation toward me, he gave rise to a heart of sincere truth and obtained such a reward."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, speaking in verse: “This one person,
having conceived a mind of joy upon seeing me,
At the end of his life was reborn in heaven, As if casting off a heavy burden.”
"If one feels even a moment of joy in their heart toward a Dharma teacher, a Tathāgata, or a bhikṣu, the fruit obtained shall likewise be so.

When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, the elder Śuka went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and with immeasurable joy, offered various praises, exclaiming that such a thing had never before occurred.
Having spoken these words, he stood to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Śuka, saying:
"This dog Śaṅkha is indeed your father."
The householder replied:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Just as the Buddha has spoken, it is true and not false; all my doubts have been completely severed."
At that time, the elder Śuka addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“All sentient beings differ in their lifespans—some short and some long; they differ in having illness or being free from it; they differ in being handsome or ugly; they differ in their lineages—noble or lowly; they differ in being intelligent or dull-witted; and they differ in being gentle or coarse. Since these matters are not uniform, how do the causes and effects of good and evil manifest as retribution?”
The Buddha said to the householder’s son Śuka, “Excellent, excellent!
You should listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall now speak for you.”

All sentient beings perform actions and cultivate causes that vary in their goodness or evil; consequently, the retributions they receive differ in terms of nobility or meanness, high or low status, and distinctions in lineage and rank are likewise diverse. I have now briefly explained such matters; were one to analyze their meaning in detail, it would be profoundly deep.
At that time, the elder addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will expound this.
Then the Buddha said to the elder:
“You should listen well!
All sentient beings create various kinds of karma and give rise to various kinds of delusions.

The karma of sentient beings is either black or white, and their retributions are accordingly divided into good and evil: black karma results in retribution within the three miserable realms, while white karma invariably brings about rebirth among humans and devas.”
Furthermore, karma has its limits, and thus lifespans are either short or long.
Moreover, individuals possess karma that results in being frequently ill or rarely ill, and being handsome or ugly.
Furthermore, there is karma by which individuals experience wealth and nobility, poverty, intelligence and wisdom, or dullness of faculties and ignorance.
Furthermore, there is karma by which individuals are born into the three evil destinies.
Furthermore, there are karmas that lead to birth in the human or celestial realms of the desire realm, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, there are karmas whereby a person travels far or near. Furthermore, there are karmas whereby a person’s aspirations are not fulfilled;
and furthermore, there are karmas whereby things arrive spontaneously without being sought.
Furthermore, there are actions such that for a certain person, success is difficult or easy to achieve, and whether it is accomplished or not.
Moreover, there are actions such that for a certain person, the lifespan in hell is either full or cut short prematurely, with varying degrees of severity.
Furthermore, there is karma such that for a person (pudgala), the sequence of wealth and poverty is not fixed;
or again, there is karma such that for a person, wealth and poverty, as well as the inclination toward generosity or parsimony, are not fixed.
Furthermore, there are actions such that the lifespan of a person (pudgala) is indefinite within them;
or again, there are actions such that the physical and mental happiness or suffering of a person is indefinite.
Furthermore, there is karma by which a person (pudgala) has a physical form that is handsome, radiant, and pleasing, or by which they have a form that is ugly, coarse, and loathsome.
Furthermore, there is karma by which a person’s faculties are either complete or incomplete, and so forth.
At that time, the Buddha said to the son of the householder,
"There are ten wholesome courses of action that you should cultivate, and there are ten unwholesome courses of action that you should eliminate.
Thereupon, the householder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Sentient beings have short lifespans; by what karma is this obtained?
The Buddha addressed the son of the householder, saying:
"It is obtained through killing. Furthermore, there are ten types of karmic action of killing:

first, killing with one's own hand; second, inciting others to kill; third, killing with a sense of joy; fourth, killing with sympathetic approval; fifth, killing while pregnant; sixth, inciting an abortion; seventh, killing to avenge a grievance; eighth, killing by castrating; ninth, killing through various means; and tenth, killing by employing others."
These ten types of actions result in the retribution of a short lifespan.
Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the retribution of a long lifespan?
There are ten such types of karma.

What are these ten? First, abstaining from killing with one's own hand; second, abstaining from inciting others to kill; third, abstaining from rejoicing in killing; fourth, abstaining from taking pleasure in killing; fifth, rescuing those facing execution; sixth, releasing living beings; seventh, bestowing fearlessness upon others; eighth, compassionately caring for the sick; ninth, generously giving food and drink;
tenth, making offerings of banners and lamps. By practicing these ten kinds of deeds, one obtains the retribution of long life.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the retribution of much illness?
There are ten types of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, destroying sentient beings oneself; second, exhorting others to destroy them; third, rejoicing in such destruction; fourth, praising such destruction; fifth, being unfilial toward one's parents; sixth, harboring many long-standing grudges; seventh, administering poison with a malicious intent; eighth, being stingy with food and drink; ninth, showing contempt for the sages and worthies;
tenth, slandering the Teacher and the Dharma. Through these ten kinds of actions, one receives the retribution of much illness.
"Furthermore, what karma results in obtaining the retribution of having few illnesses?
There are ten kinds of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, not harming sentient beings; second, exhorting others not to harm them; third, not rejoicing in harm; fourth, not praising harm; fifth, refraining from taking pleasure in harm; sixth, filially supporting one’s parents; seventh, honoring teachers and elders; eighth, not harboring old grudges; ninth, bestowing peace and comfort upon the Sangha; tenth, giving medicine and food and drink.
By these ten kinds of actions, one obtains the retribution of having little illness.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in an ugly rebirth?
There are ten types of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, constantly giving rise to anger and resentment; second, indulging in arrogance; third, being unfilial toward one's parents; fourth, constantly yielding to greed and delusion; fifth, slandering the sages and worthies; sixth, encroaching upon, seizing, and oppressing others; seventh, stealing the Buddha’s radiance; eighth, mocking the physical flaws of others; ninth, destroying the Buddha’s radiance; tenth, practicing non-celibate conduct.
Through these ten kinds of actions, one receives the retribution of ugliness.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the retribution of physical beauty?
There are ten kinds of karma.
What are these ten kinds of karma?"

First, practicing loving-kindness and patience; second, making offerings to Buddha-stūpas; third, sweeping and cleaning stūpas and temples; fourth, repairing and adorning monasteries; fifth, embellishing Buddha images; sixth, filially supporting one’s parents; seventh, placing faith and respect in the sages and worthies; eighth, being humble and free from arrogance; ninth, maintaining the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) without deficiency; tenth, staying far away from harming others.
By these ten kinds of practice, one obtains the retribution of physical beauty and dignity.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in birth into a lowly lineage?
There are ten kinds of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, coveting fame and profit while failing to practice giving; second, envying the prosperity of others; third, slighting and disparaging one’s parents; fourth, failing to follow the teachings of one’s teachers; fifth, slandering the virtuous and good; sixth, associating with evil friends; seventh, encouraging others to commit evil; eighth, destroying the goodness of others; ninth, trading in scriptures and sacred images; tenth, lacking faith in the Triple Gem.
Through these ten types of conduct, one receives the retribution of lowly birth.
"Furthermore, by what karma does one attain noble lineage and wealth?
There are ten kinds of karma. What are these ten?"

First, to be free from envy and to rejoice in the fame and profit of others; second, to respect one’s parents; third, to have faith in and honor the teacher and the Dharma; fourth, to resolve upon the bodhicitta; fifth, to offer parasols to the Buddha; sixth, to cultivate the adornment of stupas and temples; seventh, to repent of evil karma; eighth, to extensively practice acts of giving; ninth, to exhort others to cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action; tenth, to have faith in and honor the Triple Gem.
By these ten kinds of actions, one obtains the retribution of noble and wealthy status.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in an evil retribution among human beings?
There are ten kinds of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, indulging in arrogance; second, showing disrespect to one's parents; third, showing disrespect to śramaṇas; fourth, showing disrespect to brahmins; fifth, slandering the virtuous and good; sixth, showing disrespect to one's kinsmen; seventh, not believing in cause and effect; eighth, despising and detesting oneself;
ninth, hating and resenting others; tenth, not believing in the Triple Gem. These ten types of actions result in evil retribution in the human realm.
"Furthermore, what karma results in the most excellent retribution among human beings?
There are ten kinds of karma. What are these ten?"

First, being humble and free from pride; second, honoring one’s parents; third, honoring śramaṇas; fourth, having faith in and revering brāhmaṇas; fifth, cherishing and protecting one’s kinsmen; sixth, honoring the noble and holy ones; seventh, practicing the ten wholesome actions; eighth, not treating any person with contempt; ninth, honoring the teacher and the Dharma; tenth, having true faith in the Triple Gem.
By these ten kinds [of conduct], one obtains the supreme retribution among human beings.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the retribution of being solitary and poor?
There are ten kinds of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, habitually committing theft; second, inciting others to commit theft; third, praising theft; fourth, rejoicing in theft; fifth, slandering one's parents; sixth, slandering the sages and worthies; seventh, obstructing the giving of others; eighth, envying the fame and profit of others; ninth, being stingy with wealth and goods;
tenth, disparaging the Triple Gem—by these ten kinds of actions, one receives the retribution of perpetual poverty and hunger.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the acquisition of great merit?
There are ten kinds of karma. What are these ten?"

First, abstaining from theft; second, abstaining from inciting others to wrongdoing; third, abstaining from rejoicing in acts of theft; fourth, filially supporting one’s parents; fifth, placing faith in and revering the sages and worthies; sixth, celebrating the fame and profit of others; seventh, extensively practicing giving; eighth, not being envious of fame and profit; ninth, not being stingy with wealth and treasures, but showing compassion and care for the orphaned and the poor;
tenth, making offerings to the Triple Gem. These ten kinds of conduct yield vast merit.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the retribution of being dull-witted?
There are ten kinds of karma.
What are these ten kinds of karma?"

First, this person does not believe in śramaṇas nor does he associate with them; second, he does not believe in brāhmaṇas; third, he does not believe in the teacher’s Dharma nor does he associate with it; fourth, he conceals the Dharma and does not transmit it; fifth, he seeks out the faults of the teacher’s Dharma; sixth, he distances himself from the True Dharma; seventh, he cuts off and extinguishes wholesome dharmas; eighth, he slanders and reviles the virtuous and wise; ninth, he practices and studies what is not the Dharma; tenth, he slanders right view and extols wrong view. Through these ten dharmas, one obtains the retribution of dullness and stupidity.
"Furthermore, by what karma does one attain great wisdom?
There are ten kinds of dharmas.
What are these ten dharmas?"

First, this *pudgala* associates with *śramaṇas* and seeks the Dharma with deep faith; second, they have faith in *brāhmaṇas*; third, they associate with teachers and the Dharma to seek the profound meaning; fourth, they honor the Triple Gem; fifth, they distance themselves from ignorance; sixth, they do not slander the teacher or the Dharma; seventh, they seek profound wisdom; eighth, they transmit the Dharma to benefit sentient beings so that it may never be extinguished; ninth, they distance themselves from what is contrary to the Dharma;
tenth, they extol right view and remain free from all false views. By means of these ten dharmas, one attains great wisdom.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in retribution in the hells?
There are ten types of dharmas. What are these ten?"

First, unwholesome physical action; second, unwholesome verbal action; third, unwholesome mental action; fourth, constantly giving rise to the view of a self; fifth, constantly giving rise to the view of extremes; sixth, never ceasing from false views; seventh, committing evil without repentance; eighth, engaging in sexual misconduct; ninth, slandering the noble and holy ones;
tenth, destroying and extinguishing the True Dharma. Through these ten karmas, one receives retribution in the hells.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in rebirth as an animal?
There are ten types of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, a middling degree of evil physical karma; second, a middling degree of evil verbal karma; third, a middling degree of evil mental karma; fourth, giving rise to various forms of greed; fifth, giving rise to various forms of hatred; sixth, giving rise to various forms of delusion; seventh, practicing unrighteous giving; eighth, performing incantations and malevolent arts; ninth, disparaging the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) of Bodhisattvas; tenth, giving rise to the view of eternalism or nihilism, such as the belief that after death one becomes a human again. Through these ten karmas, one receives retribution as an animal.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in rebirth as a hungry ghost?
There are ten kinds of such karma. What are these ten?"

First, mild evil physical karma; second, mild evil verbal karma; third, mild evil mental karma; fourth, being stingy with wealth and property and failing to practice giving; fifth, giving rise to great false views and slandering the Buddha and the law of cause and effect; sixth, relying on one's own pride to slight and disparage the virtuous and good; seventh, obstructing the giving of others; eighth, showing no compassion for those who are hungry or thirsty; ninth, being miserly regarding food and drink and not offering them to the Buddhas and the Sangha;
tenth, using expedient means to alienate others when they obtain fame or profit. Through these ten karmas, one receives retribution as a hungry ghost.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma results in rebirth among humans?
There are ten types of karma.
What are these ten types of karma?"

First, abstaining from taking life; second, abstaining from taking what is not given; third, abstaining from unchaste conduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from frivolous and impure speech; sixth, being free from divisive speech; seventh, abstaining from harsh and abusive speech; eighth, abstaining from drinking alcohol and eating meat; ninth, abstaining from delusion and darkness; tenth, abstaining from wrong views and having sincere faith in the Triple Gem.
By cultivating these ten kinds of gentle karma, one obtains rebirth among human beings as the retribution.
"Furthermore, by practicing what karma does one attain birth among the gods of the desire realm?
By practicing the ten wholesome karmas, one attains birth in those heavens.
Moreover, by practicing what karma does one attain birth in the form realm?"
By practicing the ten wholesome meditative concentrations, one attains birth in those heavens.
Furthermore, by practicing what karma does one attain birth in those four formless realms?
By taking the cultivation of *samāpatti* as the cause, one attains birth in those heavens.

What are the four? One distances oneself from all forms, conceives of infinite space, further cultivates that meditative concentration to subdue and eliminate its obstacles, and after the end of life, is reborn in that sphere of Infinite Space.

Having distanced oneself from coarse consciousness and brought forth subtle consciousness, one forms the perception of the infinite to suppress and eliminate its obstacles; then, further cultivating that concentration, one is subsequently reborn in that heaven.
Having distanced oneself from the defilements and obstacles of the sphere of nothingness, one further cultivates that concentration and is subsequently reborn in that heaven.

Having distanced oneself from those obstacles and further cultivated that concentration, after the end of one's life, one attains rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, by practicing what kind of karma does one not arise in the Avīci hell?
By cultivating various wholesome karmas and dedicating them toward one's aspirations, one will certainly be reborn among the various auspicious realms and will not enter the Avīci hell.
Furthermore, what kind of karma must be cultivated to bring about what kind of fruit?
If one cultivates wholesome karma, one will experience desirable results; if one commits unwholesome karma, one will experience undesirable results.

If one distances oneself from these wholesome and unwholesome karmas, desirable and undesirable results can ultimately not be obtained, just as, for example, when a compassionate daughter or a merchant leader travels far away and does not return home for a long time, her children have no way to obtain her.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma does not bear fruit?

If one turns the mind to confess the evil karma one has cultivated, realizing one's former errors and reflecting with a sense of revulsion, and if one applies the mind with focused attention and sincerity to repent both in thought and speech—then although this karma was committed, its fruit will not be received;
the same applies to wholesome karma."
Furthermore, what kind of karma results in the perfection of body and mind?

By practicing patience, one attains the perfection of physical marks; by practicing hearing and reflection, one attains the perfection of the mind. Through the cultivation of this karma, the fruit will certainly be obtained.
Furthermore, what kind of karma, once cultivated and performed, is not lost?

If there is wholesome karma that, having been performed, is neither regretted nor disparaged, and is neither disturbed by affliction nor denied as non-existent; if one does not speak of its right or wrong and does not abandon it, nor act with agitation—practicing in such a manner, this karma will never be lost through cultivation, and its fruit will certainly be experienced.
"Furthermore, what kind of karma does not yield its fruit?
Cultivating indeterminate (avyākṛta) karma does not yield its fruit.
Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person (pudgala) to have a lifespan in hell without dying prematurely?"

When such a person has performed those actions, they feel no regret nor do they feel aversion; they do not deny [the law of karma], their mind is not disturbed, and they neither criticize others nor act with agitation. Devaputra, you should know that a person who performs such various actions will be born in hell and will complete their full lifespan there rather than dying prematurely.
Furthermore, what kind of karma is it such that there is a person whose lifespan is not full while dwelling in hell?

This person, having committed that karma, subsequently feels regret; through affliction, they destroy [the habit of wrongdoing], reflect upon their former errors, distance themselves from that karma, and do not act with agitation. By practicing in this manner, once this person has committed that karma, their lifespan in hell will not be full.
Furthermore, what kind of karma is it such that a person dies immediately after being born in hell?

This person, having performed that karma, feels regret and resentment, becoming agitated and saying, "I have denied [the truth]," and thus loosens and distances himself from the sharp edge of the afflictions, thinking, "This is not to be desired; I shall not do it again."
For example, King Ajātaśatru, having committed the sin of patricide, repented and confessed his transgression, saying:
"I have committed an evil deed and must suffer its consequences myself.
He then repented before the Buddha, explaining his former error.
The Buddha, out of compassion for that king, caused him to contemplate the nature of sin: that it arises illusorily from conditions and is ultimately unfindable.
Consequently, this *pudgala*, while still within the hell realms, immediately passed away.
Furthermore, what kind of karma is it whereby a person first experiences happiness and later experiences suffering?
This person initially practices giving with love, joy, and delight, but after having given, their mind feels regret.

Therefore, this *pudgala* is born among humans in a superior lineage, fully endowed with gold, silver, precious gems, elephants, horses, and carriages; his parents, wife, children, officials, subjects, and friends are complete and lacking nothing, even his storehouses are likewise so.
Consequently, when he attains the fruit [of his actions], he first experiences happiness and only thereafter undergoes suffering.
Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person to first experience poverty and suffering and later attain happiness?
Such a person, during the time of past causes, practiced giving with a low-grade mind and in small measure; having given, they felt no regret and subsequently rejoiced.

Therefore, this person is born among humans into a lowly lineage, lacking both food and precious treasures and possessing no autonomy; yet later, their wealth gradually increases until it becomes vast, and they eventually lack for nothing in various necessities. Thus, when this person attains the fruit at a later time, they first experience poverty and suffering, followed by the enjoyment of happiness.
Furthermore, what kind of karma is it whereby a person experiences happiness first and also experiences happiness later?
This person does not feel joy before giving, feels joy while giving, and feels joy after having given; thus, they have no regret during these three times.

This person is born among humans into a wealthy and noble family, fully endowed with parents, wife, children, officials, subjects, and kinsmen; they possess storehouses filled with treasures, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and even gardens, fields, and houses, all of which they enjoy with complete mastery. Thus, this person experiences happiness first and will experience happiness later as well.
Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person (pudgala) to have no happiness at first and no happiness later, constantly experiencing suffering and affliction?

This person initially lacks the intention to give, nor do they have virtuous friends who encourage them to practice generosity; moreover, lacking faith, they are greedily attached to precious treasures and never give away even the slightest thing from beginning to end.

Therefore, if this *pudgala* is born among humans, they will dwell in a low caste and experience poverty and hardship; they will lack wealth, food and drink, fields and houses, and even basic necessities, as well as all kinsmen and attendants. Having no happiness before and no happiness after, this *pudgala* suffers affliction first and suffers affliction later as well.
Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person (pudgala) to attain great wealth and nobility, yet be so stingy with their possessions that they do not give even a tiny fraction away?

This person, in past lives, practiced giving toward the Three Jewels but did not make a vow to further cultivate the practice of giving in future lives. Consequently, after this person’s death, if they are reborn among humans, they will attain great wealth and nobility, belonging to a high-ranking lineage with vast treasures; elephants, horses, servants, cattle, sheep, fields, and houses will all be extensive, and they will enjoy them with complete mastery. Yet, regarding these possessions, they will be miserly, protective, and withhold them from being given as gifts. Therefore, while this person possesses great wealth and nobility, they are protective and greedy, and furthermore lack faith.
Furthermore, by what karma does a certain person (pudgala) experience poverty and suffering in one lifetime yet delight in giving?

This person, in a past life, practiced giving toward the supreme field of the Three Jewels and made a vow; thus, his intention to give remained uninterrupted into the future. After his death, he was reborn among humans and devas, coming and going while receiving blessings. When that merit was exhausted, he was again born among humans in poverty, yet he still delights in giving. Therefore, this person remains poor yet loves to give, and his faith never falters.
Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person (pudgala) to be poor and suffering throughout a lifetime, while remaining stingy and greedy, such that they do not practice even the slightest giving?

This person, in past lives, did not encounter virtuous friends and was further mired in ignorance, failing to believe in cause and effect; thus, they did not cultivate even a fraction of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Consequently, after the end of this life, this person is born among humans into a destitute family, lacking all wealth, food and drink, fields, and necessities. For this reason, this person remains impoverished and distressed, finding no pleasure in practicing generosity.
"Furthermore, by what karma does one obtain physical and mental happiness like that of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), and moreover, delight in performing meritorious deeds?

This person, in past lives, practiced the precept of non-killing and bestowed fearlessness upon others; furthermore, they made vows with an undimmed intention to give. Therefore, after this sentient being’s life ends, they are born among humans, obtaining physical and mental happiness and constantly loving to practice generosity."

Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person to possess physical and mental happiness, yet—like an elderly person who has long abandoned worldly affairs—takes no pleasure in performing meritorious deeds?

This individual, in past lives, bestowed fearlessness upon others, refrained from harming sentient beings, and did not make superior vows; therefore, after the end of this life, this person is born among humans and attains both physical and mental happiness, having no desire to cultivate merit.
*The Scripture on the Discrimination of the Retribution for Good and Evil*, Volume Upper;
*The Scripture on the Discrimination of the Retribution for Good and Evil*, Volume Lower.
Translated at the Guhyavana Monastery in the kingdom of Jālandhara, Central India.
The Tripiṭaka Master Mingjiao, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Tianxizai, translated by Imperial Decree:
Furthermore, what kind of karma is it such that there is a *pudgala* who experiences neither physical nor mental happiness, and moreover does not cultivate merit?

This sentient being, in past lives, harmed and distressed other beings, causing them fear; furthermore, lacking faith, they did not make virtuous aspirations. Consequently, after this *pudgala* passes away, they are reborn among humans with a body and mind that lack peace, and being largely mired in ignorance, they do not practice generosity.
"What is meant by a person whose life is short in the human realm but long in the three miserable destinies?

This individual, having cultivated causes in the past, produced little merit conducive to a favorable rebirth and much evil conducive to subsequent suffering; therefore, this person’s life is brief among humans, yet their lifespan becomes long once they are born later in the hells, as hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras."
"What is meant by a person whose life is short in the three miserable realms but long among humans?

This person, having cultivated causes in the past, produced little evil conducive to rebirth in the next life but much goodness conducive to subsequent lives; therefore, this person’s lifespan in the three miserable realms is short, while their lifespan when subsequently born among humans is long."
"What kind of *pudgala* has a short lifespan when born among humans or within the three miserable realms?

This *pudgala*, having cultivated causes in the past that were both wholesome and unwholesome in small measure—both those ripening in the present life (*upapadyavedanīya*) and those ripening in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*)—therefore, this *pudgala* has a short lifespan among humans and within the three miserable realms."
"What is the person for whom both life and afflictions are exhausted?
What is the person for whom afflictions are exhausted but life is not?
These refer to those of the nature of certainty—stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners—as well as Arhats who are not yet of the nature of certainty."

"Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person (pudgala) to be born in the miserable realms (durgati), yet possess a physical form and stature that is upright, magnificent, and exquisite, such that all who see them rejoice and everyone loves them?"

This individual, having practiced the conduct of patience in past lives, violated the pure precepts of the Buddha and fell into the miserable realms to receive a body of a different species; yet his physical form was dignified and graceful, fully endowed with softness and luster, such that all who saw him were filled with joy.
Furthermore, what kind of karma causes a person to be born in the evil destinies with a body that is coarse and rough, with an ugly form and appearance, such that people find it unpleasant to behold?

This means that this person, having been by nature prone to anger in past lives and failing to cultivate the perfection of patience, violated the Buddha’s pure precepts and did not confess them; consequently, after the end of his life, he was reborn among a different class of beings, with an ugly form and coarse, rough body, deficient sense faculties, filled with foul odors, increased delusion and mental darkness, such that those who see him find no pleasure.
"Furthermore, how do the ten unwholesome karmas yield their fruits?
Taking life as the cause, one’s lifespan, physical appearance, and strength will not be fulfilled.
Stealing results in frost, hail, locusts, famine, drought, and floods."
That which is obtained through illicit desire results in much external defilement and an unchaste wife;
that which is obtained through falsehood results in a foul odor and an evil reputation, such that all people loathe and despise one;
that which is obtained through divisive speech results in disharmony among one's kin and being entangled by illness.
That which is obtained through harshness results in fruits that are hard, rough, and unpleasant to the touch;
that which is obtained through impurity results in forests thick with thorns and gardens left in ruin;
and that which is obtained through craving results in meager storehouses.
That which is obtained through hatred has a fruit that is pungent and bitter in taste, and its appearance is ugly;
that which is obtained through delusion has an impure exterior color and fruit that is hollow and withered;
these are the results obtained due to the ten unwholesome karmas.
"What are the fruits obtained by practicing the ten wholesome actions?
By abstaining from killing, the basis for one's lifespan is fully perfected;
by abstaining from stealing, calamities such as famine, windstorms, hail, and locusts are entirely eliminated."
Because of the absence of sexual misconduct, one’s fine reputation spreads far and wide, remaining free from defilement;
because of the absence of false speech, one’s mouth is always fragrant and pure;
because of the absence of divisive speech, one’s kin and retinue are harmonious and compliant, remaining far removed from the calamities of thunder, lightning, frost, and hail.
Because there was no harshness or malice, the flavor of the fruits was sweet and delicious;
because they were free from hardness and astringency, and because there was no impurity, the forests, groves, and gardens were devoid of thorns and entirely lush and moist;
because there was no craving or attachment, the storehouses and granaries were filled to capacity with fruit.
Because of the absence of ill-will, one’s physical marks are perfect and the sense faculties are without deficiency;
because of the absence of wrong views, one’s faith remains uninterrupted, and one is fully endowed with the fragrant and exquisite flavor of the supreme fruit.
Such is the ripening of the fruits of practicing the ten wholesome actions.
"Furthermore, there are ten fruits obtained from the ten unwholesome actions.
What are these ten? Regarding the ten [fruits] of killing: "

First, enemies multiply; second, those who see one are displeased; third, sentient beings are struck with fear; fourth, one constantly experiences suffering and affliction; fifth, one constantly contemplates the karma of killing; sixth, one sees sorrow and pain in dreams; seventh, one feels regret at the time of death; eighth, one’s lifespan is short; ninth, the mind and consciousness are dull and ignorant; tenth, after death, one falls into hell.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of retribution for stealing.

What are these ten? First, one binds a grudge from the past; second, one is constantly filled with suspicion; third, evil friends follow after one; fourth, virtuous friends distance themselves; fifth, one violates the pure precepts of the Buddha; sixth, one is punished by the laws of the king; seventh, one indulges in wantonness and dissipation; eighth, one is perpetually troubled by anxiety; ninth, one lacks self-mastery; and tenth, after death, one enters hell.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of retribution for perverse desire.

What are these ten? First, the mind of desire is fiercely intense; second, one's wife is not chaste or virtuous; third, unwholesome states increase; fourth, wholesome dharmas are extinguished; fifth, sons and daughters are wanton and unrestrained; sixth, wealth and resources are secretly dissipated; seventh, the mind is full of suspicion and doubt; eighth, one distances oneself from virtuous friends; ninth, one's kinsmen do not have faith; tenth, at the end of life, one falls into the three miserable realms.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of retribution for false speech.

What are these ten? First, one's breath is perpetually foul; second, one is shunned by upright people; third, one's deceitfulness increases daily; fourth, non-human beings draw near; fifth, one's sincere words are not believed; sixth, one possesses meager wisdom; seventh, one praises what is unreal; eighth, one does not utter truthful speech; ninth, one delights in debating right and wrong; tenth, after the body perishes, one falls into an evil realm.
Furthermore, there are thirty-six faults of drinking alcohol.
What are these faults?
First, the loss of wealth; second, the manifestation of many diseases; third, the provocation of strife and contention; fourth, the increase [of afflictions]...
1. One commits many killings; 2. The five [afflictions] increase one's anger; 3. One frequently fails to achieve one's intentions;
4. Wisdom gradually diminishes; 5. Merit does not increase; 6. Merit instead decreases further; 7. One reveals secrets; 8.
One’s undertakings do not succeed; 9. One greatly increases sorrow and suffering; 10. The various faculties become dull and obscured.
14. Dishonoring one’s parents; 15. Not respecting śramaṇas; 16.
Not having faith in brāhmaṇas; 17. Not revering the Buddha; 18. Not respecting the Saṅgha and the Dharma;
19. Associating with evil friends; 20. Abandoning virtuous friends; 21. Forsaking food and drink; 22. ...
12. The physical form is not concealed; 13. lustful desire is intense; 14. people do not find him pleasing; 15.
he frequently indulges in idle talk and laughter; 16. his parents are displeased; 17. his kinsmen and retinue despise him; 18.
he upholds what is contrary to the Dharma; 19. he distances himself from [the virtuous].
The True Dharma: thirty, disrespecting the noble and virtuous; thirty-one, committing transgressions and offenses;
thirty-two, distancing oneself from Nirvana; thirty-three, increasing in madness and delusion; thirty-four, mental and physical distraction;
thirty-five, committing evil through negligence; thirty-six, at the dissolution of the body and end of life, falling into the great earth.
"In hell, one suffers endless pain.
At that time, the Buddha told the elder Śuka:
"If there is another person who joins their palms in reverent worship before a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall possess ten merits."

What are the ten? First, the greatness of noble lineage; second, the greatness of exquisite physical form; third, the greatness of physical appearance; fourth, the greatness of the four requisites; fifth, the greatness of precious wealth; sixth, the greatness of a fine reputation; seventh, the greatness of the faculty of faith; eighth, the greatness of mindfulness; ninth, the greatness of wisdom; and tenth, the greatness of arts and crafts.
Thus it is, householder!
If there is another person who joins their palms in reverence before a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain this merit.
Furthermore, if there is another person who joins their palms and prostrates before a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain ten merits.

What are these ten? First, speech that is gentle and soft; second, wisdom that transcends the masses; third, being a source of joy for humans and devas; fourth, the vastness of merit and virtue; fifth, dwelling together with the virtuous and good; sixth, noble status and sovereign mastery; seventh, constantly encountering the Buddhas; eighth, drawing near to Bodhisattvas; ninth, rebirth in the heavens at the end of life; tenth, swiftly realizing parinirvāṇa. Such are the merits;
by prostrating before a Buddhist stūpa, one obtains such rewards as these.
"If there is another person who cleanses a Buddhist stūpa, they shall obtain ten merits.

What are these ten? First, the perfection of physical marks; second, a body that is smooth and straight; third, a subtle and wondrous voice; fourth, freedom from the three poisons; fifth, roads free of thorns and brambles; sixth, being of the highest lineage; seventh, noble status and sovereignty; eighth, rebirth in heaven at the end of life; ninth, a body free from defilement; and tenth, the swift realization of parinirvāṇa."
Such are the merits of sweeping and cleaning a Buddha stūpa, which yield such rewards.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who offers a parasol as a gift to a Tathāgata’s stūpa, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit.

What are these ten? First, freedom from feverish affliction; second, a mind free from distraction; third, becoming a sovereign of the world; fourth, vastness in arts and crafts; fifth, immeasurable merit and virtue; sixth, attaining the status of a Wheel-Turning King; seventh, perfection of the physical marks; eighth, distancing oneself from the three miserable realms; ninth, rebirth in heaven at the end of life; tenth, swiftly realizing parinirvāṇa.
Such are the merits obtained as retribution for offering a parasol to the Buddha.
"If there is another person who offers bells and chimes at a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit.

What are these ten? First, incomparable physical beauty; second, a wondrous voice that brings delight; third, a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird; fourth, soft and gentle speech; fifth, being met with joy by all whom one sees; sixth, attaining the vast learning of Ānanda; seventh, noble status and sovereignty; eighth, the widespread dissemination of one's good name; ninth, frequenting the celestial palaces; and tenth, the ultimate realization of parinirvāṇa."
Such are the merits obtained as the superior retribution for the gift of bells and chimes.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who offers gifts of banners and streamers at a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall possess ten merits.

What are these ten? First, a physical form that is upright, tall, and endowed with a full lifespan; second, being held in high esteem by the world; third, having roots of faith that are firm and steadfast; fourth, filially supporting one’s parents; fifth, having a vast circle of friends, relatives, and kin; sixth, possessing a beautiful reputation praised by all; seventh, having a countenance that is dignified and handsome; eighth, bringing joy to all who behold one; ninth, being born into a wealthy, noble, and sovereign family, or as a deva in heaven; and tenth, swiftly realizing parinirvāṇa.
Such are the merits obtained as retribution for offering banners and streamers to the Buddha.
"Furthermore, if there is a person who makes an offering of clothing at a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain twelve kinds of sublime merit.

What are these twelve? First, the body is straight and upright; second, all who see them rejoice; third, the marks of their fortune are radiant and moist; fourth, their physical appearance is exquisite; fifth, their form and color are peerless; sixth, their body is free from dust and grime; seventh, their clothing is fresh and clean; eighth, their bedding is fine and soft; ninth, they attain great sovereignty; tenth, at the end of life, they are reborn in the heavens; eleventh, all who see them love and respect them; and twelfth, they swiftly realize parinirvāṇa."
Such are the merits of offering robes to a Buddha, which yield such a reward.
Furthermore, if there is a person who offers flowers as an act of worship at a stūpa of the Tathāgata, there are ten merits.

What are these ten? First, their physical appearance is like that of a flower; second, they are peerless in the world; third, their faculty of smell is unimpaired; fourth, their bodies are free from foul odors; fifth, they possess pure and wondrous fragrances; sixth, they are reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions to behold the Buddhas; seventh, they are perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts; eighth, they are held in profound esteem by the world and attain the great joy of the Dharma; ninth, they are born in the heavens with sovereign ease; tenth, they swiftly realize parinirvāṇa.
Such are the merits obtained as fruits from making offerings of flowers to the reliquary stūpas of the Buddha.

“Furthermore, if there is a person who offers a floral garland as a gift to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit. What are these ten? First, their complexion will be as exquisite as a garland;

second, their body will be free from foul odors; third, their physical form will be pure; fourth, they will be born in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; fifth, the fragrance of their precepts will be aromatic; sixth, they will constantly perceive wondrous scents; seventh, their retinue will be complete; eighth, their faculties will be harmonious and joyful; ninth, they will be born in the heavens with sovereign ease; and tenth, they will swiftly realize nirvāṇa.”
Such are the merits obtained from making offerings of garlands to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, resulting in such retribution as this.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who makes an offering of lamps to a stūpa containing the relics of the Buddha, they shall obtain ten merits.

What are the ten kinds? First, the purification of the fleshly eye; second, the attainment of the pure divine eye; third, freedom from the three poisons; fourth, the acquisition of all wholesome dharmas; fifth, the possession of intelligence and wisdom; sixth, the distancing from ignorance and delusion; seventh, not falling into the three dark realms of suffering; eighth, noble status and sovereignty; ninth, rebirth among the devas; tenth, the swift realization of parinirvāṇa.
Such are the merits obtained by making offerings of lamps to the stūpas of the Buddha’s śarīra, resulting in these superior rewards.
“If there is another person who offers powdered incense as an offering to a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain ten merits.

What are these ten? First, the faculty of the nose becomes pure; second, the body is freed from foul odors; third, the body is exquisitely fragrant and clean; fourth, one’s physical form is upright and dignified; fifth, one is revered by the world; sixth, one delights in the Dharma and is widely learned; seventh, one attains noble sovereignty; eighth, one’s reputation spreads far and wide; ninth, upon the end of life, one is reborn in heaven; and tenth, one swiftly realizes parinirvāṇa.”
Thus, by offering powdered incense as an act of charity to a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata, one obtains these ten kinds of superior rewards.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who offers exquisite music to a Buddha-stūpa, they shall obtain ten kinds of sublime and excellent merits.

What are these ten? First, a physical form that is dignified and majestic; second, inspiring joy in all who behold it; third, a voice that is subtle and exquisite; fourth, speech that is harmonious and compliant; fifth, limbs and body that are at ease and pleasant; sixth, freedom from anger and resentment; seventh, rejoicing in extensive learning; eighth, noble status and sovereign mastery; ninth, rebirth in the heavens after the end of life; and tenth, the swift realization of parinirvāṇa.
Such are the merits obtained as retribution for making offerings to a Buddha stupa with sublime music.
"Furthermore, if there is a person who joyfully praises a stūpa of the Tathāgata, they shall obtain eighteen kinds of supreme and wondrous merits.

What are these eighteen? First, noble lineage; second, handsome and dignified appearance; third, a perfectly full and straight physique; fourth, bringing joy to all who see or hear them; fifth, immeasurable wealth and resources; sixth, a vast retinue; seventh, freedom from dispersal and ruin; eighth, noble sovereignty; ninth, constant rebirth in Buddha-lands; tenth, widespread renown; eleventh, praise for their virtuous qualities; twelfth, abundance in the four requisites of life; thirteenth, offerings from devas and humans; fourteenth, becoming a wheel-turning monarch; fifteenth, long life; sixteenth, a body as firm as diamond; seventeenth, rebirth in the heavens at the end of life; and eighteenth, swiftly realizing parinirvāṇa."
By thus joyfully praising the Buddha’s śarīra stūpas with such merit, one obtains this supreme retribution.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who offers a seat to the Buddha, they will obtain ten kinds of merit.
What are these ten? First, one’s virtuous deeds will be honored;

second, one will be praised by the world; third, one’s limbs and joints will possess great strength; fourth, one’s reputation will be heard afar; fifth, one’s virtues will be extolled in song; sixth, one will experience peace, harmony, and joy; seventh, one will obtain the throne of a Wheel-Turning King with a vast retinue of attendants; eighth, all who see one will rejoice; ninth, one will be born in the heavens, endowed with sovereign power and auspicious marks;
tenth, one will swiftly realize parinirvāṇa. Such are the merits obtained as superior rewards for giving a bed and seat to the Buddha.
Furthermore, if there is a person who gives shoes as an offering to the Sangha and the Buddha, they shall have ten merits. What are these ten? First, one becomes a model of dignified conduct;

second, one lacks for nothing in elephants and horses; third, one is courageous and robust when traveling on the road; fourth, the body knows no fatigue; fifth, the feet suffer no injury while walking; sixth, one avoids thorns, brambles, sand, and gravel; seventh, one attains the supernormal power of the divine feet; eighth, one has a large retinue of servants; ninth, one is born in heaven with sovereign ease; and tenth, one swiftly realizes parinirvāṇa.
Through such merit as this, one who gives shoes as an offering to the Buddha, the bhikṣus, and others, shall obtain such a reward.
Furthermore, if there is someone who offers bowls, utensils, and articles to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, their merit shall consist of ten aspects.

What are the ten kinds? First, a radiant and lustrous physical form; second, the possession of utensils for use according to one's wishes; third, freedom from hunger and thirst; fourth, an abundance of precious treasures; fifth, distancing oneself from the evil realms; sixth, being joyfully welcomed by humans and devas; seventh, the perfection of auspicious marks of merit; eighth, noble status and sovereignty; ninth, constant rebirth among the devas;
and tenth, the swift realization of parinirvāṇa. Such are the merits obtained as retribution for the gift of utensils.
“Furthermore, if there is a person who provides offerings of food during a fast-day meal to the Buddha and the assembly of monks, there are ten merits.

What are these ten? First, longevity is extended; second, physical form and complexion are perfected; third, the limbs and joints possess great strength; fourth, memory is such that nothing is forgotten; fifth, wisdom and eloquence are attained; sixth, all who behold them rejoice; seventh, precious treasures are abundant; eighth, one attains mastery among humans and devas; ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in heaven; tenth, one swiftly realizes parinirvāṇa.”
These ten kinds of supreme and wondrous merits are obtained by one who offers a meal as an almsgiving to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Furthermore, if there is another person who gives elephants, horses, and carriages as gifts to the Buddha and the Sangha, their merit shall likewise consist of ten [kinds].
What are these ten? First, feet that are soft and supple;

second, perfect and flawless deportment; third, a body free from fatigue; fourth, dwelling in peace and happiness without illness; fifth, being far removed from enemies; sixth, mastery over the divine powers (*ṛddhipāda*); seventh, having a large retinue of servants; eighth, being seen with joy by all humans and devas due to marks of merit; ninth, being reborn in the heavens at the end of life; and tenth, swiftly realizing parinirvāṇa.
Such are the merits obtained by giving vehicles—chariots, elephants, and horses—to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, resulting in such rewards.
"Furthermore, if there is a person who constructs and adorns rooms, houses, halls, and pavilions as offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, how are the characteristics of their manifold merits?
They will forever be free from fear and anxiety, with peace and happiness in body and mind;
the bedding and furnishings they obtain will be fine, soft, and most exquisite."
Their clothing shall adorn their bodies with fragrance, purity, and cleanliness;
they shall possess sovereign mastery over the five desires of the human and celestial realms;

and whether among the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa great clans, or as elders, householders, officials, merchant leaders, village heads, city governors, kings, or ministers, they shall all fully accomplish the fulfillment of their wishes.
If one wishes to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, according to the power of one's merit, ruling over one continent, two continents, or even all four continents with sovereign transformation;

or if one wishes to achieve rebirth among the gods of the six desire realms—from the Four Great Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven—may these aspirations all be fulfilled, and may one be born there at will.

Furthermore, if there are those who, by the power of their previous merit, are reborn according to their wishes in any of the heavens of the Form Realm—from the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue and the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven—they shall all achieve this.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who fully accomplishes all [attainments] from the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception within the Formless Realm;
or if they accomplish, as appropriate, the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arhat, or the state of a Pratyekabuddha, up to Unsurpassed Bodhi—[they shall likewise attain it].
Such distinctions in merit are immeasurable; by constructing chambers, halls, pavilions, and towers as offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, one obtains such retribution.
Furthermore, if there is anyone who offers fine drinks and medicinal decoctions to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit.

What are the ten kinds? First, the perfection of the sense faculties; second, purity and freshness; third, a broad and level forehead; fourth, a serene and joyful countenance; fifth, a radiant and lustrous complexion; sixth, the perfection of merit; seventh, freedom from hunger and thirst; eighth, being far removed from the three evil realms; ninth, rebirth in heaven with sovereignty; and tenth, the swift realization of parinirvāṇa.
By offering fine drinks and medicinal decoctions to the Buddha and the Sangha, one obtains such rewards as these merits.
"If there is another person who takes refuge in the Buddha and leaves the household life, they possess ten merits.

What are these ten? First, they are far removed from wives; second, they do not crave defiled desires; third, they delight in tranquility; fourth, all Buddhas rejoice; fifth, they remain far removed from malevolent spirits; sixth, they draw near to the Buddhas to hear the Dharma; seventh, they are far removed from the three evil realms; eighth, they are loved and respected by the devas; ninth, at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the heavens; tenth, they swiftly realize parinirvāṇa."
These ten kinds of merit are the rewards obtained by one who goes forth into homelessness having taken refuge in the Buddha.
"If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in solitude within the forests and wilds, he possesses ten kinds of merit."

What are these ten? First, being far removed from clamor and bustle; second, purity and fragrance; third, the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); fourth, being cherished by all Buddhas; fifth, freedom from untimely death; sixth, extensive learning and the power of retention (*dhāraṇī*); seventh, the accomplishment of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; eighth, the non-arising of afflictions (*kleśa*); ninth, rebirth in heaven at the end of life; and tenth, the swift realization of parinirvāṇa.
A bhikṣu dwelling in the forest who practices in this manner shall obtain such rewards as these.
"If there is a bhikṣu who carries his almsbowl to beg for food, there are ten kinds of merit.

What are the ten? First, his deportment is flawless; second, he brings sentient beings to maturity; third, he remains free from arrogance; fourth, he does not crave fame or profit; fifth, his field of merit is universal; sixth, all Buddhas rejoice; seventh, he causes the Three Jewels to flourish and prosper; eighth, his holy life is perfected as he abandons inferior intentions; ninth, at the end of his life, he is reborn in heaven; tenth, he ultimately attains parinirvāṇa."
Such merits as these are obtained by one who constantly maintains the alms bowl and begs for food.
If a bhikṣu maintains the alms bowl and begs for food, he remains far removed from ten kinds of darkness and first attains these ten kinds of merit. What are the ten?

First, knowing whether entering or leaving a village is beneficial or not; second, knowing whether walking among clans is beneficial or not; third, knowing whether preaching the Dharma is beneficial or not; fourth, knowing whether attending upon an ācārya or upādhyāya is beneficial or not; fifth, knowing whether transforming and benefiting sentient beings with a compassionate mind is beneficial or not; sixth, knowing whether to associate with or distance oneself from others is beneficial or not; seventh, knowing whether practicing the training in morality, concentration, and wisdom is beneficial or not; eighth, knowing whether accepting robes offered by donors is beneficial or not; ninth, knowing whether carrying the alms bowl through the streets and alleys is beneficial or not;
tenth, knowing whether using bedding and medicinal decoctions until the end of one’s life is beneficial or not. By understanding these things, one attains these ten kinds of supreme rewards.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder’s son Śuka, saying:

“Karma arises because of karma; karma ceases because of karma. Karma has distinctions of priority and sequence, as well as of projecting and completing; thus, retributions range from high to low, and the gap between the foolish and the wise is vast.”
When this Dharma was being taught, the householder Śuka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Among the Uppasaka clan of this city of Śrāvastī, and among all other clans such as the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas, upon hearing this they will all rejoice, remember it, and uphold it. We and our kinsmen shall all love and delight in it, attaining peace and happiness for a long night, benefiting ourselves and others without end."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent, Householder Śuka!”
"It is as you have said.

When the Blessed One had spoken these words, the householder Śuka, son of the Tuṇḍila clan, along with the bhikṣus and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of humans and non-humans, rejoiced and leaped for joy; they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
The Sutra on the Discernment of the Retribution of Good and Evil, Scroll II.
